extracted.intended_audience: editors, copyeditors, proofreaders, authors, and publishers
extracted.subtask_description: Stylebook rules for italics, quotation marks, capitalization, treatment of foreign/Latin words, musical and computer typography, and compound/hyphenation conventions for copyediting and typesetting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize foreign words on first occurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: A foreign word or phrase need be italicized only on its first occurrence; if it appears only rarely, however, italics may be retained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After first occurrence set in roman; retain italics for rare occurrences. See related guidance on familiar foreign words and translated terms (11.3–5, 11.18).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper nouns not italicized
rubrics_metrics.description: This rule does not extend to proper nouns, which can generally appear in roman type (except for titles of books and the like).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat proper nouns in roman unless they are titles of works or otherwise specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roman for familiar words from other languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Words and phrases from another language that are familiar to most readers and listed in Webster’s should appear in roman (not italics) if used in an English context, spelled as in Webster’s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: pasha, a priori, the kaiser; German nouns that are in Webster’s are lowercased (see 11.39).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent treatment when familiar and unfamiliar foreign terms co-occur
rubrics_metrics.description: If a familiar term should occur in the same context as a less familiar one, either both or neither should be italicized to maintain internal consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: mise en scène (familiar) and mise en bouteille (less familiar) — italicize both or neither.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roman for common Latin words and abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonly used Latin words and abbreviations should not be italicized (e.g., ibid., et al., ca., passim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: sic is best italicized because of its peculiar use in quoted matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italics or boldface for key terms on first occurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: Key terms in a particular context are often italicized on their first occurrence; thereafter they are best set in roman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occasionally boldface may be used for key terms (e.g., in textbooks or to highlight glossary terms); such usage should be noted in the text. See also 7.79 for related treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scare quotes sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks used to alert readers that a term is nonstandard, ironic, or in a special sense (scare quotes) imply distance from the term and lose force if overused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overuse. Examples: Myrotary simulation app allows me to “dial” phone numbers again. “Child protection” sometimes fails to protect. See also 7.59, 7.60.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourage using single vs double quotes to signal different functions
rubrics_metrics.description: In specialized contexts some use single and double quotation marks to signal different things, but Chicago discourages this practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a mix of italics, quotation marks, and parentheses rather than assigning different meanings to single vs double quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: "So-called" does not require quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: A word or phrase preceded by so-called need not be enclosed in quotation marks because the expression itself indicates irony or doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If calling attention to only one part of a phrase, quotation marks may be helpful. Examples: So-called child protection; Her so-called mentor induced her to embezzle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common expressions and figures of speech: no quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks are rarely needed for common expressions, figures of speech, and slang; reserve quotation marks for phrases borrowed verbatim or used ironically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Myths of paradise lost; I grew up in a one-horse town. Exception when borrowing verbatim from another context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs and notices: headline-style capitalization or quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific wording of common short signs or notices is capitalized headline-style in running text; a longer notice is better treated as a quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The door was marked Authorized Personnel Only. A longer notice should be quoted in full.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mottoes: treat like signs; foreign mottoes italicized
rubrics_metrics.description: Mottoes may be treated like signs; if the wording is in another language it is usually italicized and only the first word capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The flag bore the motto Don’t Tread on Me. Foreign example: Souvent me souviens (italicized). See also 7.53, 6.41.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words used as words: italicize or use quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: When a word or term is referred to as the word or term itself (not used functionally), it is either italicized or enclosed in quotation marks; proper nouns used as words are usually set in roman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The term critical mass is more often used metaphorically; What is meant by neurobotics? You rarely see the term iPhone with a capital i.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters as letters: italicize individual letters and combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual letters and combinations of letters of the Latin alphabet are usually italicized (the letter q; a lowercase n; a capital W).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: Traditional expressions use roman (Mind your p’s and q’s! dotting the i’s). Phonetic symbols, however, are always roman (consult Phonetic Symbol Guide).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholastic grades in roman and capitalized
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters used to denote grades are usually capitalized and set in roman type; no apostrophe required in the plural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: She finished with three As, one B, and two Cs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters standing for names: capitalization and punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: A letter used in place of a name is usually capitalized and set in roman type; if it abbreviates an actual name, it is usually followed by a period; if used to conceal a name, it may be followed by an em dash and no period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Let us assume that A sues B; Professor D. will be making his entrance shortly; Senator K— and Representative L—. If two or more initials used as an abbreviation for an entire name, no periods are needed (JFK, LBJ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters as shapes: roman capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters that are used to represent shapes are capitalized and set in roman type (an S curve, an L-shaped room).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a sans serif font sparingly for shapes may look clumsy unless it perfectly complements the serif.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of letters: set in roman without quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: The name of a letter, as distinct from the letter itself, is usually set in roman type without quotation marks; standard spellings drawn from Webster’s Collegiate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With vowels, which are not named in standard dictionaries, give an example ("a as in apple").

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhyme schemes: lowercase italic letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Lowercase italic letters, with no space between, are used to indicate rhyme schemes or similar patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Shakespearean sonnet’s rhyme scheme is abab, cdcd, efef, gg.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical pitches: roman capitals and hyphenation for sharps/flats
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters standing for musical pitches are usually set as roman capitals; the terms sharp, flat, natural, if spelled out, are set in roman type and preceded by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: middle C; the key of G major; G-sharp or G#. Use en dashes to join series of pitches (e.g., F–G–F–Bb). See also rules on octave systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Octave designation: indicate system used
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple systems exist for designating octave registers; readers should be alerted to the system employed (e.g., symbol used for middle C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of systems: lowercase with superscripts (c′, c″), lowercase with primes, or capital letters with subscripts (C, C1, C2). Technical works often use particular conventions—state which is used early in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chords and harmonic notation: roman numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: In harmony analysis, chords are designated by roman numerals indicating the degree of the scale; minor chords often use lowercase roman numerals and additional symbols or arabic numerals indicate chord quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: V (dominant), V7 (dominant seventh), iii (mediant). Harmonic progressions indicated by capital roman numerals separated by en dashes: IV–I–V–I.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynamics notation: lowercase, italics, and symbol styling
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms indicating dynamics are usually given in lowercase, often italicized (piano, mezzo forte). Symbols are rendered in lowercase bold italics with no periods (p, mf).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial dynamics added by editors may be distinguished by another font or by parentheses/brackets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application-specific vs generic treatment for computer terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Typographic conventions for names of keys, menus, commands, and similar items should follow the usage that appears with the device or software itself; generic references often require no special treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For hardware/software-specific conventions consult Microsoft/Apple style guides or the user’s guide for the specific context. See 8.155 for treatment of proper names for software and devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization for keys, menu items, and file formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic alphabet keys and all named keys are capitalized even if lowercased on a keyboard; named menu items and labels are usually spelled and capitalized as in the particular application; file-format abbreviations are rendered in full capitals unless expressed as extensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The function key F2; Option key on Mac vs Alt on PC; Save the file as a PNG or a GIF, not as a JPEG. Extensions like .html and .htm are both used for HTML files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keyboard combinations and shortcuts: plus or hyphen with no spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: To indicate simultaneous key presses use the plus sign or the hyphen with no space on either side; choice may depend on OS. Spell out Shift, Hyphen, Space, and anything else that might be ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: To save, press Ctrl+S. To save on Mac, press Command-S. To insert a double dagger on Mac: Option-Shift-7; on PC: Alt+0135 (numeric keypad).

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting off file names and text to be typed
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a combination of quotation marks and capitalization to set off file names and words to be typed or selected; punctuation that belongs to the surrounding sentence should appear outside the quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References to named items using headline-style capitalization do not usually require quotation marks. When greater prominence is desired, use bold/italics or a fixed-width font; any punctuation following such text should appear in the surrounding text font. In fixed-width text use nondirectional quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fixed-width font for typed strings, paths, and code when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: A fixed-width (monospaced) font such as Courier can signal items to be typed, directory paths, file names, variables, and other strings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any quotation marks belonging to fixed-width text should be the default nondirectional kind. Punctuation belonging to the surrounding sentence should remain in the surrounding font.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of internet/web terms: capitalize only as proper names or trademarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms related to the internet are capitalized only if they are trademarked or constitute the proper name of an organization; generic terms are lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hypertext transfer protocol (HTTP); the internet; the web; website; Wi‑Fi (trademark); Ethernet (trademark); open-source platforms. See 8.68 and 7.77 for related treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of compounds (open, hyphenated, closed; permanent vs temporary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Open compounds are spelled as separate words, hyphenated compounds include hyphens, and closed compounds are a single word. Permanent compounds are dictionary-accepted; temporary compounds are ad hoc formations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefixes and combining forms are discussed separately. For guidance first consult the dictionary; this section supplements dictionary coverage for compounds not found there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trend toward closed compounds; when in doubt opt for open
rubrics_metrics.description: With frequent use, open or hyphenated compounds tend to become closed. When unsure whether to close a compound, prefer the open form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: on line → on-line → online. Check dictionary for established usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphens improve readability and prevent ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use hyphens to show structure, pronunciation, or to eliminate ambiguity (e.g., re-creation vs recreation, co-op), but omit them where no ambiguity arises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: much-needed clothing vs public welfare administration (no hyphen needed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound modifiers before a noun: usually hyphenate
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound modifiers (phrasal adjectives) preceding a noun are usually hyphenated to lend clarity; it is never incorrect to hyphenate such modifiers before a noun (except proper nouns or adverb + adjective with -ly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the same compound follows the noun, hyphenation is usually unnecessary (e.g., a high-profile case; the case was high profile).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverbs ending in -ly: do not hyphenate
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds formed by an adverb ending in -ly plus an adjective or participle are not hyphenated either before or after a noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: largely irrelevant, smartly dressed, a highly paid ragpicker, a fully open society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple hyphens and complex modifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple hyphens are appropriate for phrases like over-the-counter drug or winner-take-all contest; if a compound modifier contains an adjective that itself modifies a compound, additional hyphens may not be necessary (e.g., late nineteenth-century literature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of readability; consult section 7.89 examples for complex cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspended hyphens for omitted second elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When the second part of a hyphenated expression is omitted, retain the suspended hyphen followed by a space (or comma in a series).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fifteen- and twenty-year mortgages; Chicago- or Milwaukee-bound passengers; do not use suspended hyphen for single entities like a five-by-eight-foot rug or ranges expressed as three-to-five-year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chicago's spare hyphenation principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Chicago prefers a spare hyphenation style: if no suitable example or analogy can be found in the section or the dictionary, add hyphens only if doing so prevents misreading or significantly aids comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 7.89 provides tables arranged by category, part of speech, specific terms, and prefixes to guide decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category-specific hyphenation rules (summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenation guidance varies by category (age terms, chemical terms, colors, compass points, fractions, money, non-English phrases, number + noun/abbreviation/percent, ordinals, time, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: Age terms hyphenated in both noun and adjective forms (a three-year-old child); chemical terms open in both noun and adjective forms (sodium chloride); colors hyphenated before a noun but open after (emerald-green tie vs his tie is emerald green); compass points closed in noun/adjective/adverb forms (north-south street). Fractions: noun open/adjective hyphenated (a half hour vs a half-hour session); money: hyphenate spelled-out units before a noun (a sixty-four-million-dollar question) but leave open after; number + noun hyphenated before a noun (a 250-page book) otherwise open; number + percent usually open except in ranges (30–40 percent). See 7.89 table for full examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation by parts of speech (summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules differ when compounds function as different parts of speech (adjective+noun, adjective+participle, adverb+participle/ adjective, noun+gerund, noun+noun, participle+noun, phrases adjectival, verbal, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General patterns: Hyphenate adjective forms before a noun; usually open after. Noun forms usually open; adjective forms hyphenated before a noun. Adverb ending in -ly + adjective/participle: no hyphenation. See section 7.89, part 2 for detailed subrules and many examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds formed with specific terms and prefixes (exceptions and standard forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific first elements (cross-, e-, email, ex-, ever-, fold, full-, general, half-, in-law, like, mid-, near-, old, on-, percent, pseudo-, quasi-, self-, step-, style, etc.) have recommended treatments—some closed, some hyphenated, some depending on Webster’s entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: email is closed; e-book, e-commerce often hyphenated or closed as listed; ex- uses an en dash if preceding an open compound; foster mother (open noun); self-restraint (hyphenated); sister-in-law (hyphenated; only first element pluralized). Check Webster’s for permanent forms; when not listed, follow the given category rules in 7.89 and section 3 examples.
